items.prompt: What is "mutation" in the sense this unit uses it?
choices: Modifying an existing object or array in place, rather than creating a new one with the change applied
Renaming a variable to something more descriptive
Converting a value from one type to another, like a string to a number
Passing a function as an argument to another function
items.explanation: Mutation specifically means changing an existing object/array's contents directly, as opposed to producing a new object that reflects the change.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, `applyPromoCode(cart, code)` set `cart.total = cart.total * 0.9`. Is this a mutation?
choices: Yes — it directly reassigns a property on the existing cart object instead of returning a new one
No — multiplying a number is never considered mutation
No — mutation only applies to arrays, not plain objects
Yes, but only because `cart` was passed as a function parameter
items.explanation: Reassigning `cart.total` changes the existing object in place — the defining trait of mutation, regardless of what kind of computation produced the new value.

items.prompt: What is "aliasing"?
choices: Two different variables (or parts of a program) holding a reference to the same underlying object, so a change through one is visible through the other
Giving a function a shorter, more convenient name
Two functions that happen to compute the same result by different means
A variable that changes type over its lifetime
items.explanation: Aliasing is specifically about shared references — not about naming or computing the same value independently.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, why did clicking "preview" change what checkout actually charged, even though preview and checkout never called each other?
choices: Both held a reference to the same cart object, so mutating it through one reference changed what the other reference pointed to as well
The two buttons secretly shared the same click handler
The server cached the discount and applied it regardless of which button was clicked
JavaScript automatically re-runs all functions that previously touched an object whenever it changes
items.explanation: Preview and checkout were aliases for the same underlying cart — there was never a second, independent copy for the mutation to be isolated to.

items.prompt: What does a function need to satisfy to be considered "pure"?
choices: Same input always produces the same output, and it produces no observable side effects
It must be written using arrow function syntax
It must not accept more than one argument
It must return a number or string, never an object
items.explanation: Purity is a behavioral guarantee — deterministic output from its inputs, and no mutation, I/O, or reliance on external state — not a syntactic style.

items.prompt: A function is written with `const` and arrow syntax, but still does `cart.total *= 0.9` inside. Is it pure?
choices: No — mutating a parameter is a side effect regardless of the syntax used to write the function
Yes — any function written with modern arrow syntax is automatically pure
Yes, as long as it doesn't call `console.log`
It depends on whether the function is exported from a module
items.explanation: Purity depends on what a function actually does, not how it's written — mutating an argument is a side effect no matter the syntax.

items.prompt: What counts as a "side effect"?
choices: Anything a function does besides computing and returning a value — mutating shared state, writing to a database, making a network call, logging
Any function that takes more than one parameter
Any function that returns `undefined`
Any function that's called more than once in a program
items.explanation: Side effects are observable changes beyond a function's return value — they're what purity explicitly rules out.

items.prompt: Is writing to a database always a mistake in a program that values immutability?
choices: No — side effects like database writes are often unavoidable; the goal is isolating them, not eliminating them entirely
Yes — a truly immutable program never performs any I/O
No, but only if the write happens inside a pure function
Yes, unless the database itself is described as "immutable"
items.explanation: Real programs need side effects to do anything useful — the practical goal is keeping them isolated in a small, clearly-marked part of the code, not avoiding them altogether.

items.prompt: What was actually wrong with the discount math in the Scenario's bug?
choices: Nothing — the math was correct; the bug was that the function mutated a shared object instead of returning a new one
The percentage was calculated backwards (multiplying instead of dividing)
The function used floating-point arithmetic, which is never safe for money
The promo code string was compared case-sensitively when it shouldn't have been
items.explanation: The 10% calculation itself was correct — the bug was entirely about mutating a shared reference, not about the arithmetic.

items.prompt: Why does immutability, as this unit frames it, matter for the Scenario's bug specifically?
choices: If `applyPromoCode` had returned a new cart instead of mutating the shared one, the preview button's call could never have affected what checkout used
Immutability would have made the discount percentage calculate faster
Immutability only matters for arrays, and the cart in the Scenario was an object, so it wouldn't have helped
Immutability prevents promo codes from being typed incorrectly
items.explanation: Returning a new object instead of mutating the shared one is exactly the fix that isolates a preview call from the real checkout state.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, before the mutating call, do `previewButton` and `checkoutStep` point to two separate cart objects?
choices: No — they both point to the exact same object; there was never a second, independent copy
Yes — each holds its own copy, and the mutation somehow copies across to the other
It depends on whether the cart was created with `const` or `let`
Yes, but the copies are synchronized automatically by the JavaScript runtime
items.explanation: The whole bug depends on there being exactly one cart object with two names pointing at it — not two separate carts kept in sync.

items.prompt: Per L2's comparison table, what's the difference in effect between a mutating and a pure version of `applyPromoCode` on other holders of the cart reference?
choices: Mutating changes what every holder of the reference sees immediately; pure leaves every other holder's reference completely unaffected
Both approaches have identical effects on other holders of the reference
Pure functions still mutate the object, just more slowly
Mutating only affects holders that called the function themselves
items.explanation: The whole point of returning a new object rather than mutating is that other references to the original object see no change at all.

items.prompt: Per L2, what are the two requirements a function must satisfy to be pure?
choices: Same input always produces the same output, and it has no observable side effects
It must not use loops, and it must return a primitive value
It must be exported from a module, and it must have a single parameter
It must run in under a fixed time limit, and it must not throw errors
items.explanation: Both conditions are necessary: determinism (same input, same output) and freedom from side effects — missing either one breaks purity.

items.prompt: A function reads `Date.now()` internally to compute part of its return value, and never mutates anything. Is it pure?
choices: No — reading `Date.now()` means the same input can produce different output at different times, breaking the "same input, same output" requirement
Yes — since it doesn't mutate anything, it automatically satisfies purity
Yes, as long as `Date.now()` is only read once per call
It depends on whether the function is called synchronously or asynchronously
items.explanation: Purity requires determinism from the arguments alone — depending on an external, changing value like the current time breaks that, even with zero mutation.

items.prompt: What is the "functional core, imperative shell" pattern?
choices: Keep calculations in pure functions (the core) and push every side effect to a thin outer layer (the shell) that calls those pure functions
Write the entire program in a functional style, with no imperative code anywhere
Use a functional programming language for the backend and an imperative one for the frontend
Wrap every function in a try/catch block to isolate errors
items.explanation: The pattern isolates side effects to a small, clearly-marked outer layer while keeping the bulk of the logic pure and easily testable.

items.prompt: Why is `computeOrderSummary` in L2/L3 easier to test than a version that also saves the summary to a database?
choices: It's pure — calling it with the same cart always gives the same result, with no database or network setup required to test it
It's shorter, and shorter functions are always easier to test
It doesn't return anything, so there's nothing to assert on
It uses `reduce` instead of a for-loop, which testing frameworks handle better
items.explanation: Purity is what makes testing trivial — no mocks, no setup, just call it and compare the output to an expected value.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, is code that uses `map`/`filter`/arrow functions automatically pure?
choices: No — a callback passed to `map` or `filter` can still mutate its argument or reach out to shared state
Yes — those methods are inherently incompatible with mutation
Yes, as long as the result is assigned with `const`
No, but only when used inside a class
items.explanation: Using functional-looking array methods doesn't guarantee purity — the callback itself can still mutate or depend on external state.

items.prompt: Per L2, is immutability free — always safe to reach for with no downside?
choices: No — returning a new object on every change has a real performance cost for large data structures, covered honestly in L3
Yes — immutability has zero performance cost in any language or runtime
No, but the cost only applies to arrays, never to plain objects
Yes, because modern JavaScript engines optimize all object copies to be instantaneous
items.explanation: L2 explicitly flags that treating immutability as free is a failure mode — the real cost for large structures is addressed honestly in L3 rather than glossed over.

items.prompt: Fix applyPromoCodePure so it returns a new cart object with the discount applied, instead of mutating the cart it was given.

tests.description: SAVE10 discounts the returned total by 10%
the original cart object is not mutated
tests.expr: expect((() => { const cart = { total: 50, discountPercent: 0 }; applyPromoCodePure(cart, "SAVE10"); return cart.total; })()).toBe(50)

tests.description: an unrecognized code leaves the total unchanged

items.explanation: Spreading `cart` into a new object and only overwriting the two changed properties means the original `cart` argument is never assigned to — every reference the caller still holds sees the unchanged original.
items.reference:
❌ Mutating — cart.total = ... changes the one shared object
✅ Pure — { ...cart, total: ... } builds a new object, leaving the original untouched

Why: a preview call and the real checkout should never be able to affect each other unless something explicitly decides to swap in the new version.

items.prompt: Fix applyPromoCodePure20 so it returns a new cart object with a 20%-off code applied, instead of mutating the cart it was given.

tests.description: SAVE20 discounts the returned total by 20%
the original cart object is not mutated
tests.expr: expect((() => { const cart = { total: 50, discountPercent: 0 }; applyPromoCodePure20(cart, "SAVE20"); return cart.total; })()).toBe(50)

tests.description: an unrecognized code leaves the total unchanged

items.explanation: Same fix regardless of the discount percentage: build a new object with spread syntax rather than assigning to properties of the argument, so the caller's original reference is never touched.
items.reference:
❌ Mutating — cart.total = ... changes the one shared object
✅ Pure — { ...cart, total: ... } builds a new object, leaving the original untouched

Why: a preview call and the real checkout should never be able to affect each other unless something explicitly decides to swap in the new version.

items.prompt: Implement toggleItemDone so it returns a NEW array with the matching item's `done` flag flipped, without mutating the original array or its items.

tests.description: the matching item's done flag is flipped in the result
tests.expr: expect(toggleItemDone([{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }], 1)[0].done).toBe(true)

tests.description: the original array's item is not mutated
tests.expr: expect((() => { const items = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; toggleItemDone(items, 1); return items[0].done; })()).toBe(false)

tests.description: non-matching items are unchanged in the result
tests.expr: expect(toggleItemDone([{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }], 1)[1].done).toBe(false)

items.explanation: `map` always returns a new array; returning a new object (via spread) only for the matching item, and the original item reference for everything else, means neither the array nor any item inside it is ever mutated.
items.reference:
🔁 map — always produces a new array, safe by default
🧩 Spread the one changed item, reuse the rest as-is

Why: this is the general pattern for updating one item in a list without touching the original list or any of its other items.

items.prompt: Implement updateItemQty so it returns a NEW array with the matching item's `qty` set to the given value, without mutating the original array or its items.

tests.description: the matching item's qty is updated in the result
the original array's item is not mutated
tests.expr: expect((() => { const items = [{ id: 1, qty: 2 }]; updateItemQty(items, 1, 9); return items[0].qty; })()).toBe(2)

tests.description: non-matching items are unchanged in the result

items.explanation: Same pattern as toggling a flag: `map` produces a new array, and only the matching item gets a new object via spread — everything else is passed through unchanged and unmutated.
